etymology: From the Hebrew cheshbon, meaning “reckoning” or “device, account”.
biblical_def: Heshbon was the royal city of Sihon king of the Amorites, who had himself wrested it from a former king of Moab. When Israel sought peaceful passage and Sihon refused, gathering his people to fight in the wilderness at Jahaz, the LORD delivered him into Israel’s hand, and they smote him and possessed his land from Arnon unto Jabbok. Thus Heshbon passed from Amorite to Israelite hands, and an ancient ballad commemorated its fall: “Come into Heshbon, let the city of Sihon be built and prepared.” The city was assigned within the inheritance east of Jordan, reckoned to Reuben and to Gad, and later numbered among the Levitical cities given to the Merarites. Centuries afterward, when Israel forfeited the land through unbelief, Heshbon reverted to Moabite and Ammonite possession and appears in the prophetic oracles against Moab. Its fame for beauty lingered: the Song likens the bride’s eyes to the fishpools of Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Heshbon stands as a monument to the LORD’s faithfulness in giving His people victory over a stubborn enemy, and to the sober truth that land held in covenant may be lost when the covenant people walk in disobedience. What God grants, He grants by grace; what He removes, He removes in righteous discipline.
webster_summary: An ancient Amorite royal city east of the Jordan, capital of Sihon, taken by Israel and assigned to Reuben and Gad.
webster_full: HESHBON, the chief city of Sihon king of the Amorites, situated east of the Jordan and north of the river Arnon.
Taken by Israel after Sihon refused passage and gave battle at Jahaz (Num 21:23).
Given for inheritance to the tribes of Reuben and Gad in the Transjordan allotment (Num 32:37).
Set apart as a city of the Levites of the family of Merari (Jos 21:39).
Its fishpools renowned for beauty, named in the Song of Solomon (Sng 7:4).
scriptures: And Israel took all these cities: and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all the villages thereof.
For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab, and taken all his land out of his hand, even unto Arnon.
Sng 7:4
Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus.
Jer 48:2

There shall be no more praise of Moab: in Heshbon they have devised evil against it; come, and let us cut it off from being a nation. Also thou shalt be cut down, O Madmen; the sword shall pursue thee.
corruption_summary: The principle worth recovering is that the LORD gives and removes inheritance according to His covenant righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Heshbon’s story preaches the providence of God over the rise and fall of nations. Sihon’s refusal to let Israel pass was not mere statecraft but the hardening of a heart appointed for judgment; the LORD “hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand.” The conquest of Heshbon was therefore an act of divine justice, not naked aggression.

Yet Heshbon also warns the covenant people. The very land won by such mercy was later lost when Israel proved faithless, passing back into Moabite hands to become a theme of prophetic lament. Inheritance is held by grace and kept by obedience; presumption upon past victories is folly. The believer learns to receive God’s gifts with gratitude and to walk humbly, lest blessings once enjoyed be removed in fatherly discipline.
roots_summary: The name derives from a Hebrew root for reckoning or accounting, fitting a fortified seat of rule and judgment.
roots_lines: Heshbon — from Hebrew cheshbon, “reckoning, account, device.”
Shares a root with the verb chashab, “to think, reckon, devise.”
The same root underlies words for a thought-out plan or invention (Ecc 7:25).
Suited to a capital where law was reckoned and rule administered.
In Scripture, men “devise” evil in Heshbon, an ironic play upon the name (Jer 48:2).
usage: The ballad of the conquest cried, “Let the city of Sihon be built,” recalling the fall of Heshbon.
Reuben and Gad pressed Moses for the rich pasture about Heshbon east of the Jordan.
Solomon, marveling at the bride, likened her eyes to the clear fishpools of Heshbon.

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps meaning “pining, wasting” or “a place of channels”.
biblical_def: Dibon lay north of the river Arnon in the territory taken from Sihon. After the conquest the children of Gad built it, so that it bore the fuller name Dibon-gad, recording the tribe that fortified and inhabited it. Yet it stood within the wider Transjordan inheritance whose borders the tribes of Reuben and Gad shared, and the city would later be reckoned to Moab once again when Israel’s grip on the eastern land slackened. Dibon figures prominently in the prophetic oracles against Moab. Isaiah foretells that Moab shall go up to the high places, even to Dibon, to weep over the ruin coming upon Bajith and Dibon; and Jeremiah summons the inhabitant of Dibon to come down from her glory and sit in thirst, for the spoiler of Moab shall come upon her. Thus the city that Gad had built became a stage for the LORD’s judgment upon Moab’s pride. Dibon teaches that no fortification, however diligently raised, can shelter a people from the hand of God when He rises to judge. The labor of men in building cities is good and lawful, but the security of any people rests not in walls but in the LORD. Moab trusted in her works and her wealth, and was brought low; the lesson endures for every nation that exalts itself against heaven.
webster_summary: A city north of the Arnon, built by the tribe of Gad and called Dibon-gad, later a Moabite stronghold named in the prophets.
webster_full: DIBON, a city east of the Jordan, north of the river Arnon, in the land taken from Sihon the Amorite.
Built by the children of Gad and hence called Dibon-gad (Num 32:34).
Reckoned within the Transjordan inheritance of Reuben and Gad.
Named in Isaiah’s oracle as a high place of Moabite mourning (Isa 15:2).
Summoned by Jeremiah to come down from her glory in thirst (Jer 48:18).
scriptures: And the children of Gad built Dibon, and Ataroth, and Aroer,
Jos 13:9
From Aroer, that is upon the bank of the river Arnon, and the city that is in the midst of the river, and all the plain of Medeba unto Dibon;
Isa 15:2
He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off.
Thou daughter that dost inhabit Dibon, come down from thy glory, and sit in thirst; for the spoiler of Moab shall come upon thee, and he shall destroy thy strong holds.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that walls and works cannot shelter a proud people from the judgment of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Dibon stands as a witness against false security. The men of Gad built it stone upon stone, and Moab afterward called it her glory; yet Jeremiah bade the daughter of Dibon come down and sit in thirst. All human industry, lawful and praiseworthy in itself, becomes a snare when men trust the work of their hands rather than the LORD who gives strength to build.

The prophets’ word over Dibon is a sermon to every age that mistakes prosperity for safety. Moab wept upon her high places too late, when judgment had already gone forth. The believer is taught to build diligently yet to hold all earthly security loosely, knowing that “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.” True refuge is found only in the covenant mercy of God.
roots_summary: The name may carry the sense of wasting away, or of channels and water-courses, fitting a town set among the streams of the Arnon highlands.
roots_lines: Dibon — from Hebrew, perhaps “pining, wasting” or “place of channels.”
Compounded as Dibon-gad to mark the tribe that built it (Num 33:45).
Possibly linked to a root suggesting flowing water or runlets.
An ironic name should the sense of wasting prove apt, given Moab’s ruin.
Distinct from a Dibon in Judah resettled after the captivity (Neh 11:25).
usage: The children of Gad built Dibon among the cities of their eastern inheritance.
Isaiah saw Moab climb to the high place of Dibon to weep over coming ruin.
Jeremiah called the proud daughter of Dibon to come down and sit in thirst.

etymology: From the Hebrew, commonly understood as “waters of quiet” or “water of rest”.
biblical_def: Medeba was both a city and the broad upland plain bearing its name, lying in the Transjordan country taken from Sihon. When the inheritance east of the Jordan was divided, the plain of Medeba fell within the portion of the tribe of Reuben, reaching from Aroer on the Arnon and including the table-land round about. It was thus part of the eastern allotment of Israel, a region of pasture and high ground well suited to the cattle of which Reuben and Gad had much. In the days of David, the children of Ammon and the hired Syrians arrayed themselves for battle before Medeba, and there Joab and Abishai routed them. Yet, like its neighbor cities, Medeba did not remain securely in Israel’s hand; it reverted to Moab and appears in Isaiah’s oracle, where Moab howls over Nebo and over Medeba, every head bald and every beard cut in mourning. The city’s history mirrors the wider Transjordan story: granted to Israel by the LORD’s victories, lost through declension, and made at last a theatre of judgment upon Moab. Medeba reminds us that the providence of God governs the bounds of every people’s habitation. He sets the tribes in their inheritance, and He removes them; the rest promised in the name “waters of quiet” is found at last not in any plain but in Christ.
webster_summary: A city and upland plain east of the Jordan, allotted to Reuben, and named among the places of Moab’s mourning in the prophets.
webster_full: MEDEBA, a city and broad table-land east of the Jordan in the territory taken from Sihon.
Assigned with its plain to the tribe of Reuben in the Transjordan allotment (Jos 13:16).
The plain of Medeba named as part of Reuben’s border (Jos 13:9).
Scene of battle when Ammon and Syria fought David’s armies (1Ch 19:7).
A place of Moabite mourning in Isaiah’s oracle (Isa 15:2).
scriptures: Jos 13:9

And their coast was from Aroer, that is on the bank of the river Arnon, and the city that is in the midst of the river, and all the plain by Medeba;
Isa 15:2
He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off.

So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people; who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that God appoints and removes the inheritance of peoples, and true rest is found only in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Medeba, whose name breathes of “waters of quiet,” teaches that the LORD “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation.” The plain given to Reuben was a real and good inheritance, yet earthly rest proved fleeting; the city passed to Moab and became a place of weeping. No portion of ground secures lasting peace.

The believer reads in Medeba a parable of the soul’s true rest. The quiet that its name promised is found not in any allotment of land but in Him who said, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” Earthly inheritances pass from hand to hand under the discipline of God; the inheritance of the saints is incorruptible, reserved in heaven.
roots_summary: The name is generally read as “waters of quiet” or “water of rest,” joining the word for water with a root for stillness.
roots_lines: Medeba — from Hebrew, “waters of quiet” or “water of rest.”

Fitting a well-watered upland plain amid the eastern table-land.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “city of brick” or “wall of potsherds” (kir, a wall or city, with a word for earthenware).
biblical_def: Kir-hareseth was a fortified stronghold of Moab, reckoned its chief refuge in the day of distress. When Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah, and the king of Edom marched against Mesha king of Moab, the LORD gave water without wind or rain and delivered Moab into their hand. The allied armies beat down the cities, marred every good field with stones, stopped the wells, and felled the good trees, until only Kir-hareseth was left standing, and the slingers compassed it about and smote it. In desperate extremity Mesha took his eldest son, who should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall — a deed of horrifying pagan despair, the dark fruit of Moab’s idolatry of Chemosh. Isaiah and Jeremiah afterward took up a lamentation over Moab in which Kir-hareseth appears, the prophet’s own bowels sounding like a harp for the ruin of the proud city. Kir-hareseth thus stands as a monument both to the LORD’s judgment upon Moab and to the bottomless cruelty into which idolatry plunges men. The Moabite king, forsaking the living God of his ancestress Ruth’s adopted people, sought salvation in the blood of his own child. The contrast with the gospel could not be sharper: there the Father gives His own Son, not in pagan terror but in redeeming love.
webster_summary: A fortified Moabite capital, the last refuge of Moab when smitten by Israel, and a city lamented in the prophets.
webster_full: KIR-HARESETH, a strong fortress and chief city of Moab, also called Kir-haresh and Kir of Moab.
Left standing alone when Israel, Judah, and Edom smote Moab’s cities (2Ki 3:25).
Besieged by slingers who compassed it about and beat it down (2Ki 3:25).
Site of Mesha’s desperate sacrifice of his eldest son upon the wall (2Ki 3:27).
Lamented by Isaiah, whose heart sounded like a harp for its ruin (Isa 16:11).
scriptures: And they beat down the cities, and on every good piece of land cast every man his stone, and filled it; and they stopped all the wells of water, and felled all the good trees: only in Kir-haraseth left they the stones thereof; howbeit the slingers went about it, and smote it.
Isa 16:7
Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl: for the foundations of Kir-hareseth shall ye mourn; surely they are stricken.
Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kir-haresh.

Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is the bottomless cruelty of idolatry, set against the redeeming love of the Father who gives His own Son.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Kir-hareseth exposes the true face of false worship. Mesha, cornered and terrified, slew his own heir upon the wall to appease the demon-god Chemosh. Idolatry always demands blood, and where it reigns it devours even children; the abominations of the heathen, which the LORD forbade Israel to learn, were never harmless folk-religion but murderous darkness.

Yet the city’s horror throws the gospel into bright relief. Where the pagan king offered his son in despairing terror to buy off a false god, the true and living God gave His only-begotten Son in sovereign love to redeem His enemies. The cross is the answer to Kir-hareseth: not man clutching at heaven by the blood of his children, but God reconciling the world to Himself through the blood of His own Son freely given.
roots_summary: The name joins kir, a wall or fortified city, with a word for brick or potsherd, marking it a city of earthen ramparts.
roots_lines: Kir-hareseth — from Hebrew kir (“wall, city”) with a term for brick or earthenware.
The element kir denotes a wall or walled stronghold (Isa 22:5).

Not to be confused with Kir of Assyria, a place of exile (2Ki 16:9).
usage: When every field was marred, only Kir-hareseth stood, and the slingers beat it down.
Upon the wall of Kir-hareseth Mesha offered his son in pagan despair.
Isaiah’s bowels sounded like a harp for the stricken foundations of Kir-hareseth.

etymology: From the Hebrew chormah, “utter destruction” or “a thing devoted to the ban,” from the root charam, “to devote to destruction.”
biblical_def: Hormah is a place whose very name preaches a sermon: “utter destruction.” Its history begins in shame. When Israel, having rebelled at the report of the spies, presumed to go up into the hill country without the LORD and without the ark, the Amalekites and Canaanites came down and smote them, beating them back as far as Hormah. There the name marked Israel’s defeat — not Canaan’s destruction but their own, for they went up in self-will after the LORD had pronounced judgment. Yet the place is redeemed in record by a later and rightly-ordered devotion. When the Canaanite king of Arad fought against Israel, the people vowed a vow unto the LORD: if He would deliver this people into their hand, they would utterly destroy their cities. The LORD hearkened, delivered up the Canaanites, and Israel utterly destroyed them and their cities, and called the name of the place Hormah — the same word now signifying victory under God’s sanction. After the conquest the men of Judah and Simeon smote the inhabitants of Zephath and devoted it likewise. Hormah thus stands as a double witness: destruction visited upon presumptuous Israel, and destruction visited by faithful Israel upon Canaan’s wickedness. The difference is obedience. The same enterprise pursued in self-will brings ruin; pursued in submission to God, it brings the promised inheritance.
webster_summary: A place in the Negeb whose name means “utter destruction,” marking both Israel’s defeat in presumption and Canaan’s devotion to the ban.
webster_full: HORMAH, a place in the south of Canaan, formerly the Canaanite city of Zephath.
The point to which the Amalekites and Canaanites beat back presumptuous Israel (Num 14:45).
Named Hormah after Israel utterly destroyed the Canaanites in answer to a vow (Num 21:3).
Smitten and devoted by Judah and Simeon in the days of the conquest (Jdg 1:17).
Its name from charam, to devote a thing to destruction under the ban.
scriptures: Then the Amalekites came down, and the Canaanites which dwelt in that hill, and smote them, and discomfited them, even unto Hormah.
Num 21:3
And the LORD hearkened to the voice of Israel, and delivered up the Canaanites; and they utterly destroyed them and their cities: and he called the name of the place Hormah.
Jdg 1:17
And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they slew the Canaanites that inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it. And the name of the city was called Hormah.
Num 21:2
And Israel vowed a vow unto the LORD, and said, If thou wilt indeed deliver this people into my hand, then I will utterly destroy their cities.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that the same work brings ruin in self-will and victory in obedience to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hormah teaches the difference between presumption and faith. When Israel went up in self-will, contrary to the LORD’s word, the name “utter destruction” fell upon their own heads, and they were beaten back. Zeal that runs ahead of God, undertaking His work without His command or His presence, ends in defeat however earnest its intentions.

The same name afterward crowned a true obedience. When Israel vowed and waited and went up under the LORD’s deliverance, Hormah became a trophy of victory. The believer learns that the worth of any labor lies not in its energy but in its submission to the will of God. To act in faith and at His bidding is to inherit; to act in presumption is to be discomfited even in a good cause.
roots_summary: The name comes from charam, to ban or devote to destruction, the same root behind cherem, the accursed thing set apart for ruin.

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps meaning “wild ass” or “fugitive,” the name of a city of the Negeb.
biblical_def: Arad was a Canaanite city in the south country, the Negeb, whose king is the first named adversary to give battle to Israel after the death of Aaron, as the people drew near the borders of the promised land. King Arad of the Canaanites, dwelling in the south, heard that Israel came by the way of the spies, and he fought against Israel and took some of them prisoners. In response Israel vowed a vow unto the LORD to devote the Canaanite cities to destruction if He would deliver them; the LORD hearkened, and the place of that devotion was called Hormah. The king of Arad is again remembered in the wilderness itinerary as the Canaanite who dwelt in the south in the land of Canaan, hearing of Israel’s approach. When at length the land was conquered and its kings enumerated, the king of Arad stands in the roll of thirty-one kings whom Joshua and the children of Israel smote on the west of Jordan. The region about Arad later received the Kenites, the kindred of Moses’ father-in-law, who went up from the city of palm trees to dwell among the people in the wilderness of Judah. Arad witnesses to the LORD’s faithfulness in subduing every king who resisted His people’s entrance into the inheritance He had sworn to give.
webster_summary: A Canaanite royal city of the southern Negeb whose king fought Israel and was numbered among Joshua’s conquered kings.
webster_full: ARAD, a Canaanite city in the south country, the Negeb, near the borders of Judah.
Its king fought Israel and took prisoners as the people approached Canaan (Num 21:1).
Named in the wilderness itinerary as the Canaanite dwelling in the south (Num 33:40).
Its king listed among the thirty-one kings Joshua smote (Jos 12:14).
Its district later settled by the Kenites, Moses’ kindred (Jdg 1:16).
scriptures: Num 21:1

And king Arad the Canaanite, which dwelt in the south in the land of Canaan, heard of the coming of the children of Israel.
The king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;
Jdg 1:16

And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which lieth in the south of Arad; and they went and dwelt among the people.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is the LORD’s faithfulness in subduing every power that resists the inheritance He has promised.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The king of Arad was the first to bar Israel’s path as they neared the land, and he took captives in his early success. Yet his name was written at last in the roll of conquered kings. The opposition that seems strong at the outset of God’s purpose is broken in the end, for no king of the Canaanites could withstand the word of the LORD to His people.

Arad encourages the believer who faces early reverses in following God. Israel suffered loss before they saw victory; the path to the inheritance ran through battle and even captivity. But the LORD who promised the land kept His word, and the king who once took prisoners was himself struck down. So the saints, however hard pressed at the beginning, shall inherit the promises through the faithfulness of God.
roots_summary: The name is variously read as “wild ass” or “fugitive,” an old Negeb place-name of uncertain final sense.
roots_lines: Arad — from Hebrew, perhaps “wild ass” or “fugitive.”

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps “strength” or “fatness,” the name both of an Amorite confederate of Abram and of the place that bore his name.
biblical_def: Mamre was the place by Hebron, marked by its oaks or terebinths, where Abram pitched his tent and dwelt and built an altar unto the LORD. It takes its name from Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and Aner, who were confederate with Abram and joined him in the rescue of Lot from the kings of the east. Mamre became one of the chief sites of patriarchal worship and fellowship with God. There the LORD appeared unto Abraham as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day, and Abraham ran to meet the three men, entertaining the LORD and His messengers and receiving the renewed promise that Sarah should bear a son. Hard by Mamre lay the field of Machpelah with its cave, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite for a burying-place, and there were buried Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah. Thus Mamre was bound up with the deepest mercies of the covenant: the appearing of God, the promise of the seed, the hospitality of faith, and the resting-place of the patriarchs in hope of resurrection. The plains of Mamre stand as a quiet emblem of the believer’s walk with God — a settled dwelling, an altar raised, communion with the LORD, and the sure hope of the inheritance that lies beyond the grave.
webster_summary: The oaks or plains by Hebron where Abram dwelt and built an altar, and where the LORD appeared to him; named for an Amorite ally.
webster_full: MAMRE, the oaks or plains by Hebron where Abram pitched his tent and built an altar (Gen 13:18).
Named for Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and Aner, confederate with Abram (Gen 14:13).
The place where the LORD appeared to Abraham in the heat of the day (Gen 18:1).
Near the field and cave of Machpelah, the patriarchs’ burying-place (Gen 23:17).
Where Jacob came to Isaac his father before Isaac’s death (Gen 35:27).

And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these were confederate with Abram.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is the pattern of the believer’s walk: a settled altar, communion with God, and hope beyond the grave.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mamre gathers up the marks of a life lived with God. Abram dwelt there and built an altar; there the LORD appeared and renewed His promise; and nearby the patriarchs were laid to rest in hope. The place is a portrait of faith at rest in the covenant, not restless and wandering but settled in worship and fellowship with the living God.

The believer finds in Mamre an enduring example. Abraham’s hospitality to the three men, his intercession for Sodom that followed, and his purchase of Machpelah as a pledge of the promised land — all flowed from communion with God in that quiet place. So the saints are called to raise the altar of worship, to walk in fellowship with their Lord, and to bury their dead in the sure hope of the resurrection promised in the everlasting covenant.
roots_summary: The name is read as “strength” or “fatness,” borne by an Amorite ally and given to the grove and plain by Hebron.
roots_lines: Mamre — from Hebrew, perhaps “strength” or “fatness, vigor.”
First the name of an Amorite, brother of Eshcol and Aner (Gen 14:24).
Transferred to the oaks or terebinths where Abram dwelt.
Identified in Scripture with Hebron in the land of Canaan (Gen 23:19).

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps meaning “goodly pasture” or “strong place,” a royal city of Bashan.
biblical_def: Edrei was one of the two royal cities of Og king of Bashan, the other being Ashtaroth. It was at Edrei that the last of the giant kings of the Amorites made his stand against Israel as they journeyed toward the promised land. When Israel turned and went up by the way of Bashan, Og the king came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. The LORD said unto Moses, Fear him not, for I have delivered him into thy hand, and all his people, and his land; and thou shalt do to him as thou didst unto Sihon king of the Amorites, which dwelt at Heshbon. So they smote him, and his sons, and all his people, until there was none left him alive, and they possessed his land. Og is remembered as a remnant of the giants, his iron bedstead a marvel of its great size. The kingdom of Bashan, with Edrei among its cities, fell to the half tribe of Manasseh in the Transjordan allotment. Edrei thus stands beside Heshbon as a twin trophy of the LORD’s victories over the Amorite kings east of the Jordan. The defeat of a giant king at a fortified city preached to Israel that no enemy, however great in stature or strong in walls, could stand against the God who fought for His people and gave them their inheritance.
webster_summary: One of the two royal cities of Og king of Bashan, where Israel defeated the giant king and took his kingdom.

corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that no enemy, however great in stature or strong in walls, can stand against the LORD who fights for His people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. At Edrei a giant king came forth with all his people, and Israel might well have feared. But the LORD said, Fear him not, for I have delivered him into thy hand. The battle was the LORD’s, and the remnant of the giants fell. Size and strength are nothing before the God who appoints the outcome of every war.

Edrei teaches the church not to measure her foes by their stature but to remember her God. The same command, Fear not, sustains the believer pressed by enemies that seem invincible. Og’s iron bedstead remained as a monument to a power that could not save him; the inheritance passed to Israel by the strong hand of the LORD. Faith looks past the giant to the One who has already given the victory.
roots_summary: The name is read as “goodly pasture” or “strong place,” fitting a chief city of the fertile and well-defended land of Bashan.

etymology: From the Hebrew beth she’an, “house of quiet” or “house of rest,” a city guarding the Jordan valley.
biblical_def: Beth-shean, also called Beth-shan, was a strong Canaanite city commanding the eastern end of the valley of Jezreel where it descends toward the Jordan. Though it lay within the allotment of Manasseh, the children of Manasseh could not at the first drive out its inhabitants, for the Canaanites would dwell in that land; and when Israel was strong, they put them to tribute but did not utterly expel them. So Beth-shean stands among the cities recorded in the sad catalogue of Israel’s incomplete obedience, where the people spared what the LORD had bidden them to remove. The most grievous scene in the city’s history came in the day of Saul’s defeat. When the Philistines had slain Saul and his sons in Mount Gilboa, they cut off his head, stripped his armour, and fastened his body and the bodies of his sons to the wall of Beth-shan, and put his armour in the house of their idols. Then the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead, remembering Saul’s kindness to them, arose and went all night and took the bodies from the wall of Beth-shan, and burned them, and buried their bones, and fasted seven days. In Solomon’s reign Beth-shean fell under one of the king’s appointed officers for provision. The city thus joins two solemn themes: the cost of failing to obey God fully in driving out evil, and the dishonor that fell upon a king who departed from the LORD.
webster_summary: A Canaanite city at the east of the valley of Jezreel where the Philistines fastened Saul’s body to the wall, and which Manasseh could not at first drive out.

corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is the cost of incomplete obedience in driving out evil, and the dishonor that follows departure from the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Beth-shean stands first as a warning against half-hearted obedience. Manasseh could not, or would not, drive out the Canaanites but put them to tribute and let them dwell in the land. Sin tolerated and managed rather than slain becomes a snare; the evil left standing in Beth-shean was a wound to Israel’s faithfulness that the LORD had commanded them to avoid.

The city’s walls bore a second, darker witness. There the body of Saul, the king who turned from the LORD and sought the witch of Endor, was hung in shame by the Philistines. Yet even there mercy appeared: the men of Jabesh-gilead honored their fallen king with a costly kindness. Beth-shean thus joins the wages of disobedience with a gleam of covenant loyalty, and bids the believer obey fully and remember the faithful even in their dishonor.
roots_summary: The name means “house of quiet” or “house of rest,” a peaceful title strangely contrasted with the city’s violent place in Saul’s downfall.

etymology: From the Hebrew, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “sandy” or “who humbles thee,” a Canaanite royal city of the Jezreel plain.
biblical_def: Taanach was a Canaanite royal city standing near Megiddo on the southern edge of the great plain of Jezreel. Its king was among the thirty-one kings whom Joshua and the children of Israel smote on the west side of Jordan. The city lay within the borders allotted to Manasseh, though it stood in the territory of Issachar and Asher, and it was set apart as one of the Levitical cities given to the Kohathites. Yet, like its neighbor Beth-shean, Taanach was not fully cleared; Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Taanach and her towns, for the Canaanites would dwell in that land. The city is most memorably recalled in the song of Deborah and Barak, where the kings of Canaan came and fought, the kings of Canaan in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, but took no gain of money, for the LORD overthrew Sisera and all his host before Barak. Thus Taanach is linked with one of the great deliverances of the period of the judges, when the LORD sold His people for their sins into the hand of Jabin and then redeemed them through a song-crowned victory. Taanach therefore witnesses both to the failure of Israel to drive out the Canaanite and to the faithfulness of God who, when His people cried unto Him, scattered the kings of Canaan by the waters of Megiddo.
webster_summary: A Canaanite royal city by the waters of Megiddo, allotted to Manasseh, made a Levitical city, and recalled in Deborah’s song.

corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that the LORD scatters the kings of the earth for His people, even where they had failed to drive out the foe.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Taanach joins the roll of cities Israel failed to clear, the Canaanites being suffered to dwell where the LORD had bidden Israel drive them out. Yet at the same waters of Megiddo, when Israel was oppressed and cried to God, He gave a great deliverance through Deborah and Barak. The same place that marked Israel’s compromise became the scene of God’s saving power.

The song of Deborah teaches that victory is the LORD’s gift, not the reward of human strength. The kings of Canaan came in array and took no gain of money, for God overthrew Sisera. So the believer, conscious of past failures to put away sin, may still cry to the LORD and find Him mighty to deliver. Where we have faltered, His faithfulness is greater than our compromise, and He fights for those who call upon Him.
